If you make players have perfect information of the opposing deck, you probably remove more skill cap rather than increase it. Why? Playing with limited information or no information requires skill in:

1. Anticipating what archetype you are up against.
2. Deciding how to mulligan.
3. Predicting what line your opponent is likely to take.
4. Understanding what your opponent has in hand, i.e., what cards to play around.
5. Knowing how to play to your own outs.
6. Evaluating the amount of tempo and card advantage.

With perfect information, you neglect most of the skills mentioned above, which creates only 1-2 lines of play to follow. Not to mention, 90% of the games would be slow and tedious control matchups that would likely end in fatigue wars. The decks would consist solely of answers and threats, and no one would be able to push through a threat for more than one turn at maximum.

In summary, removing randomness diminishes much of the skill cap, as playing around unpredictability and managing its influence is the true challenge.

Do you see the analogy?

The problem also lies in the mindset of new players. They start the game and want to reach high ranks after a month or so, and they say it's unfair that they can't do that because they keep getting matched with players who have "all top-tier decks."

Notice that according to statistics, around 75% of players are in the lower ranks, so reaching a mid-tier rank for a newer player is already a significant achievement since they are now in the group of 17.5% of players who reach mid to high ranks (technically 25% since those who end up higher also reached this rank at some point).

So there you have it. I don't want to say the ranked system is perfect, but the problem lies in people's expectations rather than an actual broken system.

It could be solved with changing the prize structure as well. As a reference, a popular trading card game has usually a pretty flat prize structure but it's awarded to the top 32, for example, or even top 64 (depending on how many players participated), because they know the game's nature is such that even the best players are not able to place in the top 4 or top 8 every time. But this also means more tournaments would have to be played in a Swiss system; this way, all the top players will have an opportunity to earn some amount from the tournaments, and those who perform exceptionally well will earn more for placing in the top 8 or better.
